stem: A 48-year-old man with occasional retrosternal chest pain undergoes exercise treadmill stress testing.  He walks for 7 minutes on the treadmill and stops due to fatigue but does not experience chest pain.  His ECG does not show any abnormal changes.  Heart rate ranges from 70/min at rest to 148/min at peak, and mean arterial pressure ranges from 95 mm Hg at rest to 112 mm Hg at peak.  Which of the following parameters was most likely decreased during peak stress compared to the resting state in this patient?​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌​​​​​‌‌​​​​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​‌​​​​​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌
explanation:
Exercise is associated with several hemodynamic and vasoregulatory adjustments to provide maximal blood flow to active muscles.  Stimulation of mechano- and chemoreceptors in the exercising muscle causes sympathetic activation and withdrawal of vagal tone, which has the following effects:

  • Venoconstriction (particularly of splanchnic veins), together with the pumping action of contracting skeletal muscle, increases venous return to the heart (ie, preload).  Healthy ventricular compliance allows the increased left ventricular end-diastolic volume (LVEDV) to be accommodated with only a small increase in end-diastolic pressure (Choice B).  Increased LVEDV increases stroke volume via myocardial stretching (Frank-Starling mechanism).

  • Increased myocardial contractility further contributes to increased stroke volume.

  • Metabolites released by exercising skeletal muscle (eg, adenosine, hydrogen ions, carbon dioxide) cause localized arteriolar vasodilation that overrides sympathetic vasoconstriction.  Meanwhile, sympathetic activation constricts splanchnic, renal, and nonexercising skeletal muscle arterioles, redirecting blood toward exercising muscle.  Because vasodilation in exercising muscle outweighs vasoconstriction elsewhere, overall systemic vascular resistance (SVR) is decreased.

  • Cardiac output (stroke volume x heart rate) is markedly increased (Choice A) due to both increased stroke volume and increased sinoatrial node firing from vagal withdrawal and sympathetic stimulation (increased heart rate).

The overall reduced SVR during exercise creates slightly decreased or unchanged diastolic blood pressure (DBP), whereas the increased stroke volume creates substantially increased pulse pressure and systolic blood pressure (Choice D); the relatively unchanged DBP accounts for only a modest increase in mean arterial pressure during exercise.

(Choice C)  Because the right and left ventricles pump in series, right ventricular output increases in parallel with left ventricular output during exercise.  Recruitment and distension of pulmonary vessels decrease pulmonary vascular resistance, but this decrease is insufficient to offset the large increase in flow, so pulmonary artery systolic pressure rises.

Educational objective:Selective vasodilation of skeletal muscle arterioles during exercise directs most blood flow toward exercising skeletal muscle and leads to overall decreased systemic vascular resistance (SVR).  Increased sympathetic tone during exercise facilitates a marked increase in stroke volume and cardiac output with a corresponding increase in systolic blood pressure, but slightly decreased or unchanged diastolic blood pressure allows for only a modest increase in mean arterial pressure.​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌​​​​​‌‌​​​​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​‌​​​​​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌
